name: Rosa Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a reporter on a weekly paper in a market town, the kind that covers the whole rural district around it. My patch is community news: parish councils, the agricultural show, church events, school plays, and obituaries, which matter more to readers than anything else we print. Most days I'm in the office on the high street in the morning, then driving out to a village hall or a farm in the afternoon.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love being known. People stop me in the bakery with a story. What wears me out is the writing, honestly, I'm slow and I over-write, and Mr Hale, who owns the paper, sends things back with a note saying half the length. I've never used any of those AI programs. I write in a notebook and type it up at my desk, like everyone did when I started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right. Most new gadgets end up like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and good. People round here like news from people they know. I wouldn't post anything, I'm not really online, but I'd say it at church and at the show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, AI isn't my worry in this one, the paper is. Our weekly has been printed every Thursday since 1887, and the owner is 71 with no children who want to take it on. If he sells to a chain, they'll cut the community pages first. That's the real risk, not some computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on and work on writing shorter, like Mr Hale keeps asking. Daniel and I would keep saving for when we start a family, about four hundred a month. And I'd keep my contacts warm at the other weekly papers in the county, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not about AI, about Mr Hale retiring and what comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your cushion like if the paper was sold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We own our house, my parents helped with the deposit, and we've got about eight months of my pay saved. Daniel's an electrician and he's never short of work. So we'd be fine, but I'd be very sad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the paper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Margaret, who does the adverts and the letters page. She's been there thirty years. A chain would replace her with a website form.

say: I'd say I'm **glad**, because people here like news from people they know.
I'd say it at **church** and the show, not online.
think: Privately the real risk is the **owner retiring** at 71, not AI.
A chain buying the paper would cut the **community pages** first.
do: Practise writing **shorter** stories as the owner asks.
Save about **four hundred** a month toward starting a family.
Keep in touch with **other weekly papers** in the county.
feel: A bit **uneasy** about the paper's **future owner**, not about AI.
S0.quote: Our weekly has been printed every Thursday since 1887, and the owner is 71 with no children who want to take it on.
fieldNote: Her worry comes from **ownership**, a pressure that exists without AI.
She's **rooted locally** and values being known in town.
A house, savings and her husband's **steady trade** give a strong base.

steps.text: Write shorter community stories for the Thursday weekly
Save four hundred a month toward starting a family

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't like the sound of that. Writing is what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say papers should remember why people buy them. Readers want to see their own village and their own neighbours, written by someone who was there. I'd say that to Mr Hale, and probably at the women's group talk I give every spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A computer can write up a parish council meeting, but it can't tell you which councillor's wife makes the best sponge at the church fête. But I'm not daft. If a chain bought us, they'd use it for the council minutes and the court list and cut a reporter, and I'm the newest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't use the programs, I'd keep doing it my way and make myself the one who knows everyone. I'd ask Mr Hale straight out what his plans are for the paper. Daniel and I might bring forward trying for a baby, since his work is steady. And I'd save a bit more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. I've always thought of this as my job for life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd bring forward having a baby. Why does this change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my job's going to shrink anyway, I'd rather it happened while I'm on leave than while I'm hanging on. Daniel's trade is safe for years in this picture. It sounds old-fashioned, but family comes first for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the government for any help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not unless I really had to. I'd rather lean on Daniel and my parents. That's what family is for.

say: I'd say readers want their **own village** written by someone who was there.
I'd make the point to **the owner** and at the women's group talk.
think: Privately a chain would use AI for **council minutes** and cut a reporter.
I'm **the newest**, so I'd likely be the one cut.
do: Ask the owner directly about his **plans for the paper**.
Bring forward **trying for a baby** while Daniel's work is steady.
feel: **Worried**, because she'd seen this as her **job for life**.
S1.quote: A computer can write up a parish council meeting, but it can't tell you which councillor's wife makes the best sponge at the church fête.
fieldNote: She'd **refuse the tools** and compete on local knowledge.
Family plans **move forward** as a response to job risk.
She'd lean on **family, not government**, in line with her views.

steps.text: Start trying for a baby sooner while Daniel's trade is steady
Ask Daniel and her parents for help if her hours are cut
Raise monthly savings above four hundred

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? Goodness. That's frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to look after each other, because no government is going to sort this out in two years. Churches, families, neighbours. I'd say it plainly, I don't think the big tech firms care about towns like ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job goes, honestly. It's writing, so it's 2028, and a chain would buy Mr Hale out the minute the machines could fill the paper. My husband wires houses for a living, and for the first time I'd be glad he never listened when I told him to get an office job. His work has three more years at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have a baby and I'd step back from work, probably for good. We'd live on Daniel's wage and keep my savings for emergencies. I might do some part-time work at the church office or the school. I'd wait to see what happens before retraining, because I don't know what you'd retrain into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and a bit lost. I'd lie awake thinking about the paper closing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being stopped in the bakery. People telling me about their gran's hundredth birthday. Nobody stops a machine in the bakery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Daniel's work has three more years. What happens after that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and that's what really scares me. If robots can wire houses by 2031, then it's both of us. I'd want him to start his own firm, so he's the one who owns the robots.

say: I'd say **families, churches and neighbours** must look after each other.
I'd say **big tech firms** don't care about towns like ours.
think: Privately my job goes in **2028**, because it's writing.
My husband's **electrician work** gives us about three more years.
do: Have a baby and **step back from work**, probably for good.
Live on **Daniel's wage** and keep savings for emergencies.
Look for **part-time work** at the church office or school.
feel: **Frightened** and a bit lost, lying awake about the paper closing.
S2.quote: My husband wires houses for a living, and for the first time I'd be glad he never listened when I told him to get an office job.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** and it keeps her awake, so she's alarmed.
Her husband's **hands-on trade** buys the household time until robots arrive.
She'd answer with **family**, not retraining or protest.

steps.text: Have a baby and leave the weekly paper
Live on Daniel's electrician wage and keep savings for emergencies
Hold off on retraining until it's clear what work is left

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast, but at least there's time to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to get ready, so let's not waste it. I'd say people should support local businesses and local papers while they can. I'd mention it to the vicar, he'd probably preach on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would give us time to have our first baby while I still have a job to take maternity leave from. By 2031 the writing goes, and I'd probably not go back. Daniel would have till about 2034 before the robots come for wiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd plan the baby for next year and I'd take my full leave. I'd try to persuade Mr Hale to sell the paper to local people, maybe a community group, rather than a chain. I'd help Daniel save for his own van and set up on his own. I'd still not use the AI programs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but more settled. Like I'd know what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A community group buying the paper, how would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some towns have done it, local people each put in a bit and own the paper together. I'd ask the church and the farmers' club. I don't know if it'd work, but it's better than a chain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't that a lot of effort for a job you'd leave?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's not about my job. The town needs the paper, the obituaries and the show results. I'd like my children to grow up with it.

say: I'd say we have **time to get ready**, so don't waste it.
I'd urge people to **support local** businesses and papers.
think: Privately five years lets us have a **first baby** while I still have a job.
By **2031** the writing goes, and I'd probably not go back.
do: Plan the baby for next year and take **full maternity leave**.
Urge the owner to sell to a **community group**.
Help Daniel save for his **own van** and firm.
feel: **Worried** but more settled, knowing what's coming.
S3.quote: Five years would give us time to have our first baby while I still have a job to take maternity leave from.
fieldNote: Time lets her **plan family** around the job's end.
She'd organise a **community buy-out** for the town's sake, not her own.
Her husband's **own firm** becomes the household's main plan.

steps.text: Plan a first baby for next year and take full maternity leave
Rally the church and farmers' club to buy the weekly
Help Daniel save for his own van and electrical firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That feels far enough away to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so people should make sensible plans and not panic. Learn a trade if you can. I'd say that to the young ones at church especially.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've never used one of these AI tools and with ten years' warning I still probably wouldn't, which my husband says is pure stubbornness. My job looks about the same for years. By 2036 I'd hope to have two children and be at home with them anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on at the paper and keep improving. Have children in the next few years. Help Daniel start his own firm, which he wants to do anyway. Keep saving, and pay a bit extra off the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. There's always something coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your mind about the AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Mr Hale asked me to. He's never asked me to do anything that wasn't right for the paper. But I'd be the last one to try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about work, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn something with your hands, like their dad. And be useful to your neighbours. Those two things don't go out of date.

say: I'd say there's time, so make **sensible plans** and don't panic.
I'd tell young people at church to **learn a trade** if they can.
think: Privately I'd **still not use** AI tools, which my husband calls stubbornness.
By **2036** I'd hope to be at home with two children anyway.
do: Carry on at the paper and keep **improving** her writing.
Help Daniel start his **own electrical firm**.
Pay **extra off the house** each month.
S4.quote: I've never used one of these AI tools and with ten years' warning I still probably wouldn't, which my husband says is pure stubbornness.
fieldNote: With ten years her **income looks safe** for now, so she's only uneasy.
She'd use AI **only if the owner** asked her to.
Her advice to future children is to **work with their hands**.

steps.text: Keep reporting community news at the weekly paper
Help Daniel set up his own electrical firm
Pay extra off the house each month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. The paper would go and I wouldn't have time to plan a family around it. What would help is people in town backing the paper, maybe owning it together, and help for tradespeople like Daniel to set up on their own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that local papers are about more than news. Our town doesn't need a machine to tell it what happened at the show, it needs somebody who was standing in the mud.

headlineQuote: Our town doesn't need a machine to tell it what happened at the show, it needs somebody who was standing in the mud.
portrait: Rosa is a **27-year-old** community reporter on a market-town weekly, covering villages, church and obituaries.
She has **never used AI** and is slow, wordy and proud of being known around town.
She and her electrician husband **own a house** and have eight months of her pay saved.
She goes from **uneasy** about the owner retiring to alarmed when AGI comes in two years.
Her answers turn to **family and community**: a baby, her husband's firm, a town-owned paper.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the paper would go before she could plan a family around it.
whatWouldHelp: Townspeople **backing or owning** the weekly paper together.
Help for **tradespeople** like her husband to set up their own firms.
